analysis.investment_thesis: CreditAccess Grameen operates an important social mission as India's leading listed microfinance institution, but it is not a Fisher investment: ROE has collapsed to 7.86%, net profit fell 63% in FY25 (INR 1,446 Cr → INR 531 Cr), OCF was negative for four of five years, and the business model structurally requires perpetual external debt funding at D/E of 2.81. The P/E of 41.8x on stress-trough earnings is unattractive regardless of the low forward multiple.
key_strengths: Revenue CAGR of 28.4% over six years reflects genuine last-mile distribution scale and India's underpenetrated rural credit market
Diversified loan product evolution (from pure group microcredit to two-wheeler, housing, digital loans) shows management building a broader financial services platform
Promoter holding of 66.28% (CreditAccess India BV) provides strong institutional backing and governance alignment
key_risks: Net profit collapsed 63% in FY25 (INR 1,446 Cr → INR 531 Cr) reflecting sector-wide MFI stress from borrower overleveraging, a structural industry risk that recurs cyclically
ROE of 7.86% is far below Fisher's 20% threshold; a business that earns 7.86% on equity while taking on 2.81x leverage is not creating economic value at scale
Regulatory and political risk is existential for MFIs: state-level interest rate caps, loan waivers, and RBI guidelines can impair the business model overnight
red_flags: OCF was negative in 4 of 5 years (2020–2024): -INR 2,253 Cr, -455, -2,713, -3,290, -4,734—the business model requires constant external debt to fund loan disbursements, creating perpetual refinancing dependency
Finance costs growing at 29.4% CAGR (INR 417 Cr → INR 1,955 Cr) outpace net profit CAGR of 8.7% over the same period—the spread is compressing structurally
Total assets declined from INR 28,871 Cr to INR 27,679 Cr in FY25—loan book contraction signals active credit stress management, not growth
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Fisher's qualitative framework was built around identifying innovative, growth-compounding businesses with expanding margins and visionary product development. Microfinance is a worthy sector but it does not fit that template. The business is a spread-compression machine during credit cycles: CreditAccess earned INR 1,446 Cr in FY24 and INR 531 Cr in FY25—a 63% drop in a single year with no warning—because the MFI sector simultaneously hit the wall on borrower overindebtedness. This cyclicality, driven by systemic borrower stress rather than company-specific execution, is exactly the kind of risk Fisher avoided.

The forward P/E of 13.65 might attract value investors anticipating earnings normalisation, but Fisher would note that this is a recovery bet, not a growth investment. The ROE of 7.86% on D/E of 2.81x means the unlevered return on assets is approximately 2-3%—not a compounding machine. Finance costs are compounding at 29.4% CAGR, faster than the business can grow revenue per rupee of equity. Until the MFI sector credit cycle fully resolves, ROE returns to 15%+, and the loan book resumes healthy growth, Fisher would deploy capital elsewhere.
